title: ‘Bad money drives out good’: people spend debased coins and hoard the valuable ones

cover.alt: Black-and-white film still from the Dutch state mint in Utrecht: a gloved worker tips a ladle of glowing molten silver into a row of moulds.

body: When two coins must be accepted at the same face value but one holds more precious metal, people keep the good coins and pay with the bad ones, until the good ones vanish from circulation. This is **Gresham’s law**, named after the Tudor financier Thomas Gresham, though Copernicus described it in 1519 and Aristophanes noticed it in *The Frogs*, usually dated to 405 BC. It works because legal tender laws act as a price control, fixing both coins at the same value. After the US Coinage Act of 1965 cut half dollars to 40% silver, the older 90% silver coins were quickly hoarded by the public.

slides.alt: Black-and-white silent film: in the Dutch state mint, gloved workers tip ladles of white-hot molten silver into a row of moulds, throwing up bright flames.
slides.caption: The Dutch state mint in Utrecht, filmed around 1916: smelters pour white-hot silver from ladles into moulds, the first step in making silver coins.

slides.heading: An old idea with a Tudor name

events.text: Aristophanes notices it in The Frogs
Copernicus describes it; Tudor financier Thomas Gresham is born
Henry Dunning Macleod names it after Gresham
US half dollars drop to 40% silver

slides.heading: Henry VIII’s shillings
slides.text: Henry VIII replaced 40% of the silver in English coins with base metals. His subjects saved the good, pure-silver shillings and spent the bad ones, exactly as Gresham’s law predicts.

left.label: Gresham’s law
left.text: Bad money drives out good when both must be taken at the same price.

right.label: Thiers’ law
right.text: Good money drives out bad when the bad money becomes nearly worthless.

slides.question: Why did Americans hoard half dollars made before 1965?
options: Banks paid a bonus for them
slides.explanation: Old half dollars were 90% silver, new ones only 40%, yet both were worth 50 cents. People kept the silver-rich coins and spent the debased ones.
